title: Batching & Cache Rollback Orchestration + Safety Audit for Optimize Auto-Tuner
creator: Marisol Chen
description: Summary: After two recent incidents where Optimize auto-tuning applied aggressive batching/cache configs that regressed p95 latency for tail-heavy workloads, we need a dedicated orchestration layer and audit checklist to make config changes safely reversible. Goal: design and implement a rollback-orchestration pattern, automated safety audit checks, and a simulation harness so future autotune proposals can be validated end-to-end before and after apply. This ticket covers design decisions, short-term mitigations, integration tests, and a playbook for on-call and SRE teams.
root_cause: The autotuner’s cost-first objective pushed batching thresholds and KV cache eviction policies that reduced token cost but increased variability in sequence-handling paths. There was no coordinated canary rollout or stateful rollback hook that could restore prior cache profiles atomically. Metrics and alerting were insufficiently sensitive to tail-latency regressions during gradual rollouts.
timeline_summary: 2025-01-27: Autotune proposal #PR-512 applied to in-production dedicated pool, initial rollout at 10% traffic
2025-01-28 03:40 UTC: p95 latency alerts fired for region eu-west-1; aborts were attempted but rollback hook failed because cache profile mismatch blocked restart
2025-01-28 06:15 UTC: Manual rollback completed after instance drain; rollback required restarting several nodes -> brief capacity dip
2025-02-05: Post-incident analysis indicated lack of atomic config swap and no simulation harness to predict tail regressions
mitigation: Immediate: Add a safety throttle on autotune proposals limiting batch-size increases to <= 15% per hour and require manual approval for >30% changes
Short-term: Add pre-apply validation that simulates 99th percentile latency on sampled production traces (see testing_plan)
Medium-term: Implement an orchestrator that performs canaries with automatic fast rollback under p95/p99 thresholds
playbook_steps: 1) Detect: Alert when p95 increases >20% over baseline or p99 increases >10% within 15 minutes of a config apply
2) Throttle: Immediately reduce autotune rollout to 0% and set a temporary global throttle if alerts persist
3) Snapshot: Capture current cache/batching profiles and KV caches where feasible (hot-keys list) before attempting any rollback
4) Rollback: Apply atomic config-swap via orchestrator; if atomic swap fails, schedule node-level drain-and-restart with traffic-shifting to standby pool
5) Post-revert verification: Run synthetic user journeys and tail-latency smoke tests for 30 minutes before marking incident resolved
6) Postmortem: Add incident to optimize-incident tracker and schedule design review within 5 business days
rollback_policy: All autotune proposals must publish a reversible plan. Reversibility requires (a) config snapshot prior to apply, (b) an atomic swap endpoint that supports rollback token within a 60-minute abort window, or (c) fallback to a stable variant model/queue. If rollback token fails, orchestrator escalates to node drain and restore flow. Rollback triggers: p95 >20% OR error rate increase >0.5% sustained for 10 minutes.
testing_plan: - Unit: validate config schema and idempotence for config-swap API
- Integration: pre-apply dry-run simulator using 24h sampled traces with current runtime kernels and KV distribution to report delta p50/p95/p99
- E2E Canary: staged rollout with dynamic canary windows (5%, 20%, 50%), automated rollback hooks active at each step
- Chaos: introduce controlled cache eviction events in staging to verify rollback and cache warmup timing
monitoring_and_alerting: - Dashboards: canary_run_overview (per-proposal) with real-time p50/p95/p99, error rate, and cost delta
- Alerts: create composite alert that combines p95 increase and increased tail queueing time
- Audit logs: every autotune proposal must write an immutable audit entry with proposal metadata, pre-apply snapshot link, and operator who approved
decisions: Adopt a two-tier approval: small deltas (<15%) auto-apply; medium deltas (15-30%) require an automated simulation pass and on-call approval; >30% require offline review and product sign-off
Implement orchestrator as an independent service (opt-orch) rather than ad-hoc scripts to ensure strong observability and idempotent rollback semantics
Prioritize building a simulation harness for real tail-latency prediction before investing in more aggressive batching heuristics
